title: Harun al-Rashid and the Youth Manjab

full_text:
Caliph Harun al-Rashid, walking through the quiet lanes of Baghdad with Vizier Ja'afar, heard sweet strains of a lute and a youth's voice singing verses of poignant beauty from a modest rooftop:
'The night is dark, the stars shine clear,
Yet sorrow holds my spirit dear;
Not for gold do I pine or sigh,
But for an honest roof beneath the sky.'

Intrigued, the Caliph climbed the exterior stairs and greeted the singer, who introduced himself as Manjab, a poor calligrapher from Basra.
Manjab welcomed the disguised strangers with warm hospitality, offering his only meal: a small dish of dates and a pitcher of cold well-water.

'Young man,' asked Harun al-Rashid, 'thy voice bears rare beauty, and thy calligraphy on yonder table is of imperial quality. Why dost thou live in such frugal poverty?'

Manjab smiled gently:
'Noble traveler, my father died burdened with debts. For five years I have labored eighteen hours each day copying manuscripts to repay every copper he owed to the merchants of Basra. Yesterday, I paid the final dinar. I have nothing left in my pocket, but tonight my heart sings with pure joy, for my father's memory is clean before God and man.'

The Caliph was deeply moved by the youth's extraordinary filial piety and unyielding integrity.
Before departing, Harun al-Rashid slipped a gold signet ring beneath Manjab's ink-stand, saying:
'Tomorrow at noon, bring this ring to the gate of the Grand Palace, and inquire for the merchant Harun.'

The next day, Manjab arrived at the palace gates, showed the ring to the captain, and was escorted into the magnificent imperial diwan.
Beholding the guest of the previous night seated upon the throne of the Caliphate, Manjab trembled and prostrated himself.

Harun al-Rashid descended from his throne, raised the young man with his own hands, and said:
'Manjab, thou hast honored thy father through honest sweat and selfless devotion. Today, the Caliphate honors thee.'

The Caliph appointed Manjab Chief Master of the Imperial Scriptoria, endowed him with an estate by the Tigris, and provided dowries for his sisters, showing that heaven never forgets those who uphold filial duty and righteous conduct.
moral: Generosity exercised in secret brings heavenly rewards; kings find true joy in elevating the humble.
